text: Every course so far in this path has treated the instance as a stable thing you build on. It isn't. ServiceNow ships major platform releases on a real, regular periodic cadence, and every customer's instances eventually move onto each new release in turn, one after another.

This isn't a one-time migration a company opts into once and never thinks about again. It's an ongoing fact of running on the platform. Each named release updates features, the UI, security defaults, and, critically, which APIs are considered current, which are deprecated, and which have been removed entirely.

ServiceNow performs the technical work of moving an instance onto a new release. But planning and validating that move is squarely the customer's responsibility. ServiceNow doesn't support every past release forever — older releases eventually reach end of support, which pressures every customer to stay reasonably current, release after release.

For anyone building scoped applications, business rules, or client scripts, an upcoming release carries a specific risk: code that quietly relies on a deprecated or soon-to-be-deprecated API. A script can run perfectly for years, right up until the release that finally removes what it depended on, and then it fails, sometimes silently. The discipline is straightforward: watch release notes for deprecation warnings, and avoid building new work against anything already flagged as on its way out.

The standard protection organizations use is a dedicated pre-upgrade sandbox — a sub-production instance that ServiceNow upgrades to the new release ahead of production, specifically so real custom applications, integrations, and customizations can be validated there first, with time to fix whatever breaks.

If a scoped application breaks under the new release, it breaks there, in a disposable sandbox, not on upgrade day in front of real users. That pattern — validate the upcoming release before the real upgrade ever happens — is the first concrete piece of application lifecycle management this course covers. Next: the broader instance strategy that pattern actually depends on.
